I enjoy traveling and eating street food. Street food, since the notion doesn't even exist in America, is people setting up shop on the side of the street and selling whatever they feel they're good at cooking. It's completely unregulated and open to anybody who can create something resembling a stand and put some food on it. I've eaten from these vendors thousands of times in my life and gotten sick exactly once - and I was just fine shortly thereafter.

And a fun thing. You can get a bag of rice, some fresh pork/chicken, and veggies. All cooked up deliciously - for about $1. The raw ingredients aren't that much cheaper than the US on the average. The difference is there's a lot less distance between the farm and your mouth thanks to a lack of burdensome rules and regulations. That gets even more literal when you have trucks that pick up the day's harvest from farms and then sell it door to door.

There's another massive difference here. In the US the vast majority of food is served by low wage employees who couldn't care less about their job other than to put some money in their pocket. That's in large part because you need approaching 6 figures to comfortably open a restaurant in the US, so you're mostly only going to have people doing it solely as an investment. When you don't need to have that large capital up front to open up a standard, the food is often sold by the people who are making up the recipes. The food is clean because the people serving it enjoy cooking, enjoy eating, and just generally enjoy food and their work.

I'm far from some sort of anarcho-cap type, but I think anybody who actually got to experience the world of food without so many laws and regulations would realize that's one area we've definitely got overboard. And not just a little bit, but way overboard.
